proposed_edges.relationship: Phantoms of Remembrance (1994) studies how eleventh-century people (women praying for their dead, monks keeping and reshaping archives, scribes choosing which royal pasts to celebrate or forget) preserved the past or formulated the past they preferred to imagine.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher description read (Princeton University Press, book page; copyright 1994, paperback 1996): the book ‘makes important new inroads into the widely discussed topic of historical memory’, describes practices of remembrance in written and nonwritten forms, gives ‘women praying for their dead, monks creating and re-creating their archives’ and scribes deciding ‘which royal families of the past to applaud and which to forget’, and shows people ‘formulating the past that an individual or group prefers to imagine’. The page quotes Alexander Murray (TLS) on ‘three case-studies’ of ‘local patterns of memory’. The book is unread; this is a publisher's account. Date confirmed by the CV entry already on the atlas (tc234_geary_cv). Replaces the memory edge held in revision 1.234 because the IAS page refused access; no claim is made about which memory theorists Geary uses.

review.reason: Princeton University Press page re-fetched: description begins 'In Phantoms of Remembrance, Patrick Geary makes important new inroads into the widely discussed topic of historical memory', with 'Women praying for their dead, monks creating and re-creating their archives, scribes choosing which royal families of the past to applaud and which to forget' and 'formulating the past that an individual or group prefers to imagine'; copyright 1994, paperback 5 May 1996. Publisher provenance acceptable. The evidence note states plainly that this is a publisher's account and the book is unread, and makes no claim about memory theorists. A book whose subtitle and description place it in memory studies supports a bounded person → field contribution.
